1.title: The Risk Practice in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module seven: The Risk Practice in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two practices. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Apply the risk practice: risk management approach, risk register. Areas of focus of key roles. Threats and opportunities, risk appetite and tolerance, the five risk steps, owners and responses. Analyze whether a risk approach is effective and fit for purpose considering the principles, the techniques and tailoring. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two practices (fifty-one percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and principles
1.text: Purpose, objectives and principles. The risk practice gives the project a structured way to deal with uncertainty. A risk is something that might happen and would affect an objective. It can be a threat or an opportunity. A risk is described by its cause, the event and the effect. If it has already happened, it is an issue, not a risk. It serves continued business justification (risks affect the case), manage by exception (risk tolerance triggers escalation), define roles (every risk has an owner), learn from experience (past risks guide identification) and manage by stages (risks are reviewed at each boundary).

1.title: Purpose, objectives and principles, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and principles. The figure shows this: The five risk steps: identify, assess, plan, implement and communicate, around the risk register. Exam tip: Might happen is a risk; has happened is an issue. If a scenario says the supplier is already late, do not treat it as a risk.

1.title: The key management products
1.text: The key management products. Risk management approach. How risk is managed on this project: roles, scales for probability and impact, risk appetite and tolerance, response types, reporting. Part of the initiation documentation. Risk register. A record of each risk: description, owner, assessment, responses, status. Part of the project log and updated all the time. Risk appetite is how much risk the organization is willing to take to reach its objectives. Risk tolerance is the limit of exposure that is acceptable at a level; beyond it, the risk is escalated. Exam tip: Approach says how; register says what. The scales and tolerances are agreed once in the approach; the individual risks live in the register.

1.title: Areas of focus of the key roles
1.text: Areas of focus of the key roles. Executive. Accountable that risk is managed and the approach suits the business case. Senior user. Risks to user needs and benefits. Senior supplier. Risks in the supplier's work and resources. Project manager. Creates the approach and register; makes sure risks are identified, assessed and controlled. Team manager. Raises risks from the work; manages those assigned. Project assurance. Checks risk procedures are followed. Project support. Keeps the register and analysis up to date. A risk owner is accountable for managing one risk and needs the authority to do it. A risk action owner carries out a response action for the owner. The owner is often not the person who does the work. Check the book's table for exact responsibilities.

1.title: Effective management and techniques
1.text: Effective management and techniques. Identify. Find risks and write them as cause, event and effect, using lessons and the people involved. Assess. Rate probability, impact and proximity (when); compare exposure with the tolerance. Plan. Choose a response; name the owner and action owners. Implement. Carry out the response and monitor its effect. Communicate. Share risk information with stakeholders; escalate what exceeds the tolerance.

1.title: Effective management and techniques, continued
1.text: Effective management and techniques. Responses to threats include avoid, reduce, fallback, transfer, accept and share. Responses to opportunities include exploit, enhance, share and reject. Reduce makes a threat less likely or smaller; transfer moves the financial impact to another party; exploit makes an opportunity more certain. After a response, some residual risk remains, and a response can create a secondary risk. Both are assessed and recorded. Risks are reviewed regularly: at each stage boundary and in routine progress reporting. Exam tip: Escalate when the exposure goes beyond the tolerance of your level. The project manager keeps risks that fit the stage tolerance and sends the rest to the board.

1.title: Judging a scenario
1.text: Judging a scenario. Each risk has an owner with authority (define roles). Risks with no owner, or the whole list owned by one person. Assessed for probability, impact and proximity. Only a vague "high or low", no timing. Opportunities recorded and managed with threats. Only threats are recorded. Reviewed regularly and at every stage boundary. Register written at initiation and never reopened.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Escalated to the right level when tolerance is exceeded (manage by exception). Project manager sits on a risk beyond the tolerance, or sends every risk to the board. Residual and secondary risks recorded. Risk closed as soon as a response is chosen. Appetite and tolerance agreed in the approach. Each person uses their own scales.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Tailoring. Small internal project. A one-page approach and short register reviewed at each checkpoint. Agile or hybrid delivery. Risks reviewed at each sprint review; the backlog carries risk-driven items. Large or multi-party project. Shared risks across suppliers, with owners named in each organization and escalation paths in the contract. Sustainability or data concerns. Sustainability, data and security risks are assessed like any other. Exam tip: A risk without an owner is not managed. The first check on any risk scenario is who owns it, then whether it was assessed, then whether it is at the right level.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. On a small internal project to update berth signs, Sam Okafor keeps a one-page risk management approach and a short risk register with named owners, reviewed at each checkpoint. Was this appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Yes, because the approach is scaled to the project while risks keep owners and review. Tailoring scales the approach, and the register keeps owners, assessment and review, which preserves the intent of the practice.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Marta Quinn agrees that Sam Okafor owns the risk of a late test environment. Wei Chen's team will order the extra environment as the agreed response. Which statement describes Wei Chen's role in relation to the risk? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: He is a risk action owner, carrying out the response for the owner. Wei carries out a response action for the owner, who stays accountable for managing the risk.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A supplier risk on Project Harbor now has an exposure beyond the project's risk tolerance, and Sam Okafor cannot respond within his authority. What should he do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Escalate it to the project board with the assessment and the options. Risk that exceeds the tolerance of the project manager's level must be escalated, as manage by exception requires.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Sam Okafor wants the agreed scales for probability and impact, and the risk appetite and tolerance, written once so everyone assesses risks the same way. Which management product holds them? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Risk management approach. The risk management approach sets scales, appetite and tolerance, while the other approaches cover issues, quality and change; the register holds the individual risks.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Tomas Reyes suggests reusing a payment module from another port, which could cut build cost. Sam Okafor records it in the risk register as an opportunity, names an owner and asks the team to assess a response. Was this appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Yes, because opportunities are uncertain events handled with the same steps as threats. The practice covers threats and opportunities, and both are identified, assessed, planned and tracked in the register.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. To reduce the risk of a late build, Sam Okafor adds a second supplier team, then marks the risk closed. The extra team might cause integration problems. What should he have done? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Record the residual and secondary risks with owners, and keep reviewing them. A response can leave a residual risk and create a secondary risk, and both must be assessed, owned and reviewed.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the five risk steps. Answer: Identify, assess, plan, implement and communicate. Question two. What is the difference between risk appetite and risk tolerance? Answer: Appetite is how much risk the organization is willing to take; tolerance is the limit of acceptable exposure at a level. Question three. Who is accountable for managing a risk? Answer: The risk owner.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is a secondary risk? Answer: A new risk created by a response to another risk. Question five. What three aspects are assessed for each risk? Answer: Probability, impact and proximity. Question six. Which risk is a risk and not an issue? Answer: One that might happen; if it has already happened, it is an issue.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Risk: threat or opportunity from uncertainty: cause, event, effect. Five steps: identify, assess, plan, implement, communicate. Assessment: probability, impact and proximity against the tolerance. Appetite and tolerance: willingness to take risk; limit that triggers escalation. Owner and action owner: owner is accountable; action owner does the action. Risk management approach: scales, roles, appetite, tolerance. Risk register: each risk, owner, responses, status. Residual and secondary: assessed and recorded after every response.
